The main idea is the point of the whole text. Every sentence supports it. A detail is just one piece of the puzzle.
Think of a news article. The main idea is the headline, not one fact from the middle of the story.
Here's the method. Say the point of the whole text in about five words, before you look at the choices.
Then cross out three kinds of wrong answers. Too small, meaning just one detail. Too extreme, meaning it goes further than the text. And never said.
Watch for the turn. Words like however, but, and a new study usually come right before the main idea.
Here's an example. People thought a cave's humming was random. However, a study found that wind blowing through one opening causes it.
The turn is, a study found. My five words: wind causes the cave's hum.
Trap alert. A choice saying visitors have always feared the cave is never said. The text doesn't mention fear at all.
Another pattern. Earlier historians saw an old herbal book as a simple guide. However, one historian sees it as both practical and moral.
The main idea comes after however. The book was more than a simple guide. The choice that says earlier historians were right picks the setup, not the point.
Let's try an SAT style question. Monarch butterflies fly three thousand miles each fall. No single butterfly makes the whole round trip. It takes several generations.
My five words: the trip takes generations. Now check the choices.
Each monarch flies three thousand miles twice? That contradicts the text, which says no single butterfly does. Cross it out.
Your turn. Pause the video. The first gummy candies looked very different. Changes over time helped them evolve into today's form. Say the main idea in five words.
Something like, the candy changed over time. A choice saying early versions would be unrecognizable today is too extreme. The text says different, not unrecognizable.
Remember three things. Main idea covers the whole text. Look after the turn. And cross out too small, too extreme, and never said. Great work.
